content: The document titled Guidelines for Establishing a Poison Centre is an updated version of the 1997 publication Guidelines for Poison Control, which was developed under the auspices of the World Health Organization (WHO). This update reflects advancements in the roles and activities of poison centres, as well as developments in information technology and communication. It also emphasizes the renewed importance of poison centres in public health, particularly following the revision of the International Health Regulations (IHR) in 2005, which require countries to have the capacity to detect, respond to, and manage public health events caused by chemicals. The guidelines provide comprehensive information on the establishment and operation of poison centres, which are specialized units that assist in the prevention, diagnosis, and management of poisoning. Poison centres primarily serve as information services, but they may also include clinical treatment units and toxicological laboratories. These centres play a critical role in public health by collecting data on poisoning cases, supporting toxicovigilance, and contributing to the sound management of chemicals. The document outlines the history of poison centres, which were first established in response to the growing need for specialized toxicology advice following the post-World War II increase in chemical products and poisoning incidents. The first poison information centre was founded in Chicago in 1953, followed by others in Europe and around the world. These centres have historically provided telephone-based advice and have evolved to include internet-based databases and surveillance systems for aggregating and analyzing poisoning data. The guidelines also address the international policy framework supporting poison centres, including their recognition as a priority in global health and environmental forums such as Agenda 21, the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management, and the WHO Chemicals Road Map. The IHR specifically identify poison centres and toxicology laboratory services as core capacities for countries to meet their public health obligations. The document provides practical guidance on setting up poison information services, clinical toxicology services, and analytical toxicology services. It also discusses the role of poison centres in toxicovigilance, chemical incident preparedness and response, antidote availability, staff training, quality assurance, and potential funding sources. Additionally, it includes annexes with resources, examples of toxicovigilance systems, and templates for operational procedures and user satisfaction assessments. The update was prepared with contributions from experts in poison centres, medical and analytical toxicology, and public health from various WHO regions. It was reviewed and revised through a collaborative process involving WHO collaborating centres, national poison information services, and other stakeholders.
